hints: Focus on what the catalytic converter is trying to make, harmless $\text{N}_2$, $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from polluting gases.
Check nitrogen in $\text{NO}$ (+2) and $\text{NO}_2$ (+4), both must end up as $\text{N}_2$ (0), so what must happen to its oxidation number?
Now look at carbon in $\text{CO}$ and in hydrocarbons, both end up as $\text{CO}_2$ (+4), so link that change in oxidation number to complete the redox pair.
walkthrough:
**Remember the job of the catalytic converter**

Think like a cleaner. We want to turn toxic gases into safe gases. That means $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{N}_2$, and $\text{CO}$ and hydrocarbons to $\text{CO}_2$ (plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$).

Typical reactions:
$$2\text{NO} + 2\text{CO} \rightarrow \text{N}_2 + 2\text{CO}_2$$

**Decide what happens to the nitrogen oxides**

In $\text{NO}$, N is +2. In $\text{NO}_2$, N is +4. In $\text{N}_2$, N is 0.

The oxidation number decreases, so electrons are gained. That is reduction:
$$\text{NO}, \text{NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{N}_2 \text{ (reduction)}$$

**Decide what happens to CO and hydrocarbons**

In $\text{CO}$, C is +2. In $\text{CO}_2$, C is +4. The oxidation number increases, so electrons are lost. That is oxidation.

Similarly, carbon and hydrogen in hydrocarbons gain oxygen to form $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. That is also oxidation:
$$\text{CO}, \text{hydrocarbons} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (oxidation)}$$

**Put the redox pair together**

One side is reduced ($\text{NO}$, $\text{NO}_2$) and the other side is oxidised ($\text{CO}$, hydrocarbons). They react with each other, so no extra oxygen is needed. This matches reduced, reduced, oxidised, oxidised.

options.A: Incorrect. This reverses the redox roles. $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ cannot be oxidised to give $\text{N}_2$ because oxidation would increase N oxidation number, not decrease it to 0. $\text{CO}$ cannot be reduced to $\text{CO}_2$ because that is an increase in C oxidation number.
options.B: Incorrect. If everything were oxidised, there would be no reduction to balance it. $\text{NO}$ (+2) to a higher state and $\text{NO}_2$ (+4) to a higher state would not give $\text{N}_2$ (0). A redox reaction needs both oxidation and reduction.
options.C: Correct. $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ are reduced to $\text{N}_2$ (N oxidation number falls to 0). $\text{CO}$ is oxidised to $\text{CO}_2$ and unburnt hydrocarbons are oxidised to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This is a balanced redox pair.
options.D: Incorrect. If everything were reduced, there would be no oxidation to balance it. $\text{CO}$ to $\text{CO}_2$ is an increase in oxidation number (+2 to +4), and hydrocarbons to $\text{CO}_2$ plus water also involves gain of oxygen, so both are oxidations, not reductions.
